headlines.article_text: Stock market today: Live updates Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Traders work at the New York Stock Exchange, Nov. 10, 2026. NYSE Stock futures ticked higher on Sunday night following a volatile week on Wall Street, as traders await a highly anticipated earnings report from Nvidia and a potentially record-setting public market debut. Nasdaq-100 futures gained 0.6%, while S&P 500 futures advanced 0.3%. Dow Jones Industrial Average futures traded 71 points higher, or 0.1%. In Asia, investors will focus on key economic data out of Japan and China Monday. Japan's Nikkei 225 futures contract in Chicago were at 61,320, compared with the index's previous close of 61,142.35. Futures for Hong Kong's Hang Seng index last traded at 23,722, compared with the index's close of 23,637.6. Australia's S&P/ASX 200 was down marginally in early trading. Nvidia is set to report results after the bell on Tuesday. While analysts expect the chipmaker to post nearly 100% year-over-year earnings and revenue growth, investors will be more focused on how the company will move forward after Jensen Huang's exit as CEO. Huang last week resigned from his post after reports of multiple extramarital affairs, including one with an alleged Chinese spy. Nvidia shares dropped 13%, marking their biggest weekly slide since April 2025. "The main task at hand for interim CEO Colette Kress [is to] restore order and give the Street confidence in the Nvidia story going forward," wrote Dan Ives, analyst at Yorkville Ives. "This starts with earnings and the conference call this week on Tuesday after the bell…we still expect guidance and a typical conference call around robust business metrics with demand metrics that have clearly accelerated since last quarter." Another key catalyst is Anthropic's initial public offering. The AI giant is eyeing a roughly $1.4 trillion valuation, with shares expected to be priced between $70 and $78. Wall Street is coming off a winning week despite Nvidia's tumble. The Dow, S&P 500 and Nasdaq posted their biggest weekly gains since August, rising more than 2% each. 5 Min Ago Nikkei 225 futures trade higher ahead of GDP data Nikkei 225 and Hong Kong's Hang Seng index were set to open higher Monday, with focus on key economic data out of Japan and mainland China. China is expected to release data for retail sales, industrial output and urban unemployment for October later in the day, while Japan will release economic growth data. Japan is expected to see GDP growth slow sharply to an annualized 0.3% for the third quarter, compared to 1.4% in the quarter before, according to Reuters estimates. Aaron Schwartz | Afp | Getty Images Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said Sunday that a router installed in southern Arkansas as part of an upgrade to a system overseen by L3Harris Technologies could be key to problems that led officials to order the biggest halt to flight departures to U.S. airports since 9/11 on Friday. "We think it was the installation or the router that was the bad actor," Duffy said in an interview with Fox News. "We're open if we see something else, we're going to continue to investigate with our federal partners and law enforcement." Duffy told ABC's "This Week" in a separate interview that the router was located in El Dorado in southern Arkansas. The equipment, along with another router that was in Amarillo, Texas, is at an L3Harris lab in Florida for examination, Duffy said. He said the router, part of ongoing work to switch from copper wire to a fiber-optic system, began flooding other systems. Federal officials said on Saturday that "instability" in communication feeds and data like radar prompted the more than four-hour ground stop. Flight disruptions lingered on Sunday but were far from the thousands of cancellations passengers faced on Friday and Saturday. There was "zero evidence" that the problem was caused by something "nefarious" or anything related to artificial intelligence, Bryan Bedford, the head of the Federal Aviation Administration, said at a press conference with Duffy Saturday morning. Bedford said no FAA facilities went dark but that officials decided to ground flights because of "instability" in information feeds to air traffic control centers that handle en route aircraft at high altitudes and eventually to others closer to airports. The issue occurred during "routine" upgrades of switching from a copper wire system to fiber, Bedford said. A router had "flooded" other routers in the air traffic control system with over 1,000 connection attempts roughly every five seconds, said Duffy. That created problems with airplane communications and radar feeds, they said. "We were unwilling to take any risk that this propagation could actually result in a center losing connectivity with aircraft," said Bedford. He said officials weren't sure for about 45 minutes what was causing the instability. The outage again thrust aging infrastructure that underpins U.S. air traffic control into the spotlight, along with the country's struggles to replace sections of it while operating the world's busiest airspace. "What we're working to determine was whether we had incompetence, meaning was it user error, installator error from L3 Harris, or did they install a faulty router," he said. L3Harris said it is "supporting the FAA in its investigation to understand the conditions that led to the Nov. 13 ground stop of our nation's air travel." The company, a longtime U.S. contractor, said it has completed more than 70% of the switch from copper wiring to fiber-optic system. Duffy took the groundstop to seek billions more from lawmakers to modernize the system. Rough weekend Flight disruptions began to ease Sunday, though more than 2,000 flights were canceled. That was down from the roughly 6,500 cancellations Saturday and over 8,000 delays, according to flight-tracking site FlightAware. That's on top of more than 9,000 U.S. flight cancellations, about a third of the day's schedule, and more than 7,000 delays on Friday, though some disruptions were due to bad weather. Friday had the second-highest U.S. flight cancellations since a severe blizzard and below-freezing temperatures in January, according to aviation-data firm Cirium.
